title: Aldehydes and Ketones I
description: Explore carbonyl electrophilicity, addition products, and oxidation–reduction.
objectives: Identify hydrates, hemiacetals, acetals, imines, and enamines

cards.rule: The carbonyl is polarized Cδ+–Oδ−. A nucleophile attacks carbon while the pi pair shifts to oxygen; protonation can then give an alcohol. Aldehydes are generally less crowded and less electron-rich than comparable ketones, so they often add nucleophiles more readily.
cards.cue: Attack C; move pi electrons to O; then handle proton transfers. Aldehydes use -al, or -carbaldehyde when CHO is attached to a ring; ketones use -one. Use oxo- for a subordinate carbonyl. Methanal/formaldehyde, ethanal/acetaldehyde, propanal/propionaldehyde, butanal/butyraldehyde and pentanal/valeraldehyde are common name pairs; propanone is acetone.
cards.trap: Neutral aldehydes and ketones can accept hydrogen bonds but lack an O–H donor. Do not draw five bonds to carbon when a nucleophile adds. A planar carbonyl can be attacked from either face. At comparable mass and shape, boiling points often follow alkane < aldehyde/ketone < alcohol; this is a trend, not a universal ordering across unrelated molecules.
cards.app: A chiral environment can favor one face; without such bias, addition that creates a single new stereocenter often yields a racemic mixture.

steps.label: 1. Find the electrophile
steps.text: The C=O carbon is trigonal planar and electron poor. Oxygen is electron rich.

steps.label: 2. Move the pi pair
steps.text: The purple curved arrow shows the carbonyl pi pair moving toward oxygen during nucleophilic attack. This arrow is one part of an addition mechanism; the incoming nucleophile is described in the lesson rather than drawn here.

rule.title: Carbonyl Polarity, Bürgi-Dunitz Attack (~107°) & Aldehyde vs. Ketone Reactivity

items.label: Permanent C=O Dipole & Resonance
items.text: Oxygen is more electronegative than carbon (R₂C=O ↔ R₂C⁺–O⁻), making the sp² carbonyl carbon strongly electrophilic (δ+) and the oxygen weakly basic/nucleophilic (δ−).

items.label: Electronic Effect (Inductive Donation)
items.text: Alkyl groups are electron-donating (EDG): a ketone has TWO alkyl groups donating electron density to reduce δ+ on carbon; an aldehyde has only ONE.

items.label: Steric Effect in the sp³ Tetrahedral Intermediate
items.text: Nucleophilic addition compresses bond angles from 120° (sp² trigonal planar) to 109.5° (sp³ tetrahedral), crowding bulky ketone R groups.

figure.caption: Carbonyl addition: encoded electron-flow arrows start at electrons and end at the accepting site.

cue.title: Acid-Catalyzed vs. Base-Catalyzed Carbonyl Addition Order
cue.prompt: Are you running carbonyl nucleophilic addition in basic or acidic conditions?

items.label: Basic / Strong Nucleophile (RMgBr, LiAlH₄, CN⁻, RO⁻)
items.outcome: Step 1: Attack C=O → Step 2: Protonate Alkoxide (O⁻)
items.text: Strong anionic nucleophiles attack the neutral C=O directly to form a tetrahedral alkoxide intermediate, then pick up H⁺ on workup.

items.label: Acidic / Weak Nucleophile (ROH, H₂O + Catalytic H⁺)
items.text: Acid protonates the carbonyl oxygen FIRST, converting a moderate electrophile into a super-electrophilic oxocarbenium ion (R₂C=OH⁺) so weak ROH can attack.

items.label: Comparing Carbonyl Boiling Points
items.text: Strong C=O dipole-dipole interactions raise BP above alkanes/ethers, but lack of O–H means no self-H-bonding (lower BP than alcohols).

trap.title: Drawing a Pentavalent Carbon or Forming O⁻ in Strong Acid

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Attacking C=O without breaking the π bond (5 bonds on C!), or drawing a strongly basic RO⁻ alkoxide intermediate in H₂SO₄.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Always push the C=O π electrons onto oxygen as the nucleophile attacks; keep intermediates cationic/neutral in acid and anionic/neutral in base!

app.title: Oxyanion Holes in Proteases & Lewis-Acid Metal Catalysis (Zn²⁺ / Mg²⁺)

items.label: Serine Protease Oxyanion Hole
items.outcome: Backbone N–H H-Bonds Stabilize Tetrahedral O⁻
items.text: Two enzyme amide N–H bonds donate H-bonds to the developing negative charge on the tetrahedral intermediate oxygen, lowering ΔG‡.

items.label: Metalloenzyme Zn²⁺ Catalysis
items.outcome: Zn²⁺ Acts as a Super-Proton on C=O
items.text: Coordination of carbonyl oxygen to Zn²⁺ polarizes the C=O bond just like acid catalysis, accelerating nucleophilic attack at pH 7.4.

items.label: IR C=O Stretch (~1715 cm⁻¹)
items.outcome: Large C=O Dipole Change → Intense Sharp Peak
items.text: Because C=O has a huge permanent dipole moment, stretching it absorbs IR radiation strongly around 1700–1750 cm⁻¹.

lessons.label: Hydrates, hemiacetals, and acetals
lessons.title: Hydrates, hemiacetals, and acetals
lessons.tag: Distinguish OH from OR on the same carbon

cards.rule: A hydrate has two OH groups on one carbon. In traditional terminology, aldehyde-derived hemiacetals have OH, OR, H and R at the former carbonyl carbon; further acid-catalyzed reaction gives acetals with two OR groups, H and R. Ketone-derived counterparts have two carbon groups and are called hemiketals (OH + OR) and ketals (two OR). Broad IUPAC acetal/hemiacetal classes also include the ketone-derived compounds. Equilibria depend on water/alcohol activities.
cards.cue: Two OH = hydrate; OH + OR = hemiacetal; two OR = acetal. Ketone-derived examples are also called hemiketals/ketals.
cards.trap: Acetal formation requires acid catalysis; base alone does not turn OH− into a good leaving group. Cyclic sugar hemiacetals can be stable because intramolecular ring formation is favorable.
cards.app: Monosaccharides cyclize through hemiacetal or hemiketal formation. The new anomeric center can have two configurations. Acetal/ketal protection can preserve a carbonyl during many basic or hydride reactions, including suitable LiAlH4 conditions. Aqueous acid restores the carbonyl; compatibility must be checked for the whole substrate.

steps.label: 1. Identify a hemiacetal
steps.text: This carbon bears both OH and OCH3, along with methyl and H. It is a hemiacetal from ethanal and methanol.

steps.label: 2. Compare a ketal
steps.text: This separate ketone-derived example is a ketal: two OCH3 groups and two carbon groups surround the central carbon. It is not the direct next product of the ethanal hemiacetal in step 1. Aqueous-acid hydrolysis regenerates a ketone.

steps.label: 3. Compare a hydrate
steps.text: Here both oxygen substituents are OH: a geminal diol. The equilibrium does not equally favor hydrates for every carbonyl.

rule.title: Hydrates, Hemiacetals/Hemiketals & Acid-Only Acetal Protecting Groups

items.label: Hemiacetal / Hemiketal Formation (1 Eq ROH)
items.text: Acid- or base-catalyzed addition of 1 ROH across C=O yields a carbon bonded to ONE –OH and ONE –OR (unstable open-chain, but favored in 5/6-membered sugar rings!).

items.label: Acetal / Ketal Formation Requires ACID (2 Eq ROH + H⁺, −H₂O)
items.text: Protonation turns the hemiacetal –OH into –OH₂⁺, which leaves to form a resonance-stabilized oxocarbenium ion (R₂C=OR′⁺) attacked by a second ROH.

items.label: Base Immunity & Acid Deprotection
items.text: Because RO⁻ cannot leave in base, acetals are 100% stable to NaOH, LiAlH₄, NaBH₄, and Grignards; hydrolyze back to C=O + 2 ROH with aqueous acid (H₃O⁺).

comparison: Reversible in H⁺ OR HO⁻; favors C=O
Forms in acid OR base; cyclic sugars stable!
Forms ONLY in ACID; locked in base/RMgBr/LiAlH₄!

figure.caption: Compare hemiacetal, ketal and hydrate connectivity. These are separate illustrative examples.

cue.title: Identify the Carbonyl Derivative by Counting Oxygen Attachments on the Same Carbon
cue.prompt: Inspect the sp³ carbon that holds two single bonds to oxygen:

items.label: Bonded to –OH and –OR (plus R/H)
items.text: Examples: α/β-D-glucopyranose at anomeric C1! Equilibrates with the open-chain aldehyde in water (mutarotation, reducing sugar).

items.label: Bonded to –OR and –OR (Two Ether Links on 1 C)
items.text: Examples: sucrose/starch glycosidic bonds or ethylene glycol dioxolane protecting group; NON-reducing and stable to base/LiAlH₄!

items.label: Bonded to ONLY ONE –OR (C–O–C on Separate Carbons)
items.text: Ordinary ethers do not hydrolyze in mild aqueous acid, whereas acetals rapidly revert to aldehydes/ketones in H₃O⁺.

trap.title: Trying to Form or Hydrolyze an Acetal in Base (NaOH / RO⁻)

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Writing RCHO + 2 CH₃OH + NaOH → Acetal, or cleaving a glycosidic acetal bond with aqueous NaOH.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: Base catalysis STOPS at the hemiacetal (HO⁻ cannot leave to form an oxocarbenium ion)! Acetals form and hydrolyze ONLY in acid (H⁺).

app.title: Carbohydrate Anomeric Carbon (Hemiacetal vs Glycoside Acetal) & Multi-Step Synthesis

items.label: Reducing vs. Non-Reducing Sugars
items.text: Maltose and lactose have one free hemiacetal C1–OH (mutarotates, Tollens +); sucrose locks both anomeric carbons as an acetal/ketal (non-reducing!).

items.label: Ethylene Glycol Acetal Shield
items.text: Protects the more reactive aldehyde/ketone as a 5-membered cyclic acetal while LiAlH₄ reduces an ester elsewhere in the molecule.

items.label: Glycogen Phosphorylase / Glycosidases
items.text: Enzymatic cleavage of glycosidic acetal bonds proceeds through a planar, resonance-stabilized oxocarbenium intermediate.

cards.rule: A primary amine condenses with an aldehyde or ketone to form an imine after addition, proton transfers, and water loss. A secondary amine can form an enamine when an alpha H is available. Related nitrogen reagents form oximes (hydroxylamine), hydrazones (hydrazine derivatives), and semicarbazones (semicarbazide). Cyanide addition followed by protonation forms a cyanohydrin and creates a C–C bond. Ammonia can also give an imine under suitable condensation conditions. An imine with an available alpha H can interconvert with an enamine tautomer by proton and double-bond relocation. Secondary-amine condensation proceeds through an iminium ion and alpha deprotonation; no N–H remains at that intermediate.
cards.cue: Primary amine → C=N; secondary amine + alpha H → C=C–N. Cyanide adds its carbon.
cards.trap: Too much acid protonates the amine and suppresses its nucleophilicity. Enamine formation needs an alpha hydrogen. Do not attach cyanide through nitrogen in a standard cyanohydrin product.
cards.app: Schiff-base (imine) intermediates help enzymes reorganize electron density; nitrogen chemistry is a bridge to amino-acid metabolism.

steps.label: 1. Imine bond
steps.text: The C=N bond replaces the starting C=O after condensation with a primary amine. This connectivity drawing does not assign E/Z about C=N.

steps.label: 2. Enamine bond
steps.text: An enamine has N attached to a C=C system. The nitrogen lone pair is conjugated with the double bond, giving nucleophilic carbon character. The displayed imine and enamine are separate examples with different substituents and formulas, not a tautomeric pair.

steps.label: 3. Cyanohydrin carbon count
steps.text: Acetone cyanohydrin contains a new C–C bond between the former carbonyl carbon and the nitrile carbon. The nitrile N is triple-bonded to that new carbon.

rule.title: Imine and enamine formation: amine class, acid catalysis and competing protonation

items.label: Primary Amine (RNH₂ / NH₂OH / NH₂NH₂) → Imine (C=N)
items.text: Nucleophilic addition forms a carbinolamine; acid protonates –OH to –OH₂⁺, and the nitrogen lone pair pushes out water to form R₂C=NR′ (imine/oxime/hydrazone).

items.label: Secondary Amine (R₂NH) → Enamine (C=C–NR₂)
items.text: After losing H₂O, the iminium ion (R₂C=NR′₂⁺) has NO proton left on nitrogen! Base removes an α-C–H proton instead to form a nucleophilic alkene-amine (enamine).

items.label: Cyanohydrin Formation (KCN / HCN)
items.text: CN⁻ attacks the carbonyl to form a new C–C bond (R₂C(OH)CN); nitrile can then be reduced to a 1° amine or hydrolyzed to an α-hydroxy carboxylic acid!

chips: Mild Acid optimum pH depends on substrate

figure.caption: Separate imine and enamine examples: different skeletons, not a displayed tautomer pair.

cue.title: Balance nucleophile availability with acid-catalyzed dehydration
cue.prompt: What happens if the pH is too high or too low during imine formation?

items.label: Too Basic (pH > 9): No H⁺ Available
items.text: Amine attacks C=O, but without acid to protonate –OH into –OH₂⁺, dehydration stalls completely.

items.label: Too Acidic (pH < 2): All RNH₂ Protonated to RNH₃⁺
items.outcome: No Nucleophilic Lone Pair Left to Attack!
items.text: Strong acid converts 100% of the amine into non-nucleophilic ammonium ions (RNH₃⁺), stopping Step 1.

items.label: Sweet Spot (substrate-dependent pH)
items.outcome: Enough Free RNH₂ to Attack + Enough H⁺ to Dehydrate
items.text: Produces the classic bell-shaped rate vs. pH profile tested on the MCAT!

trap.title: Drawing a Charged Iminium or Enamine from the Wrong Amine Class

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Forming a neutral C=NR₂ imine from a secondary amine, or calling separate imine and enamine molecules from different amines "tautomers".

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: 1° amines have 2 N–H protons → neutral Imine (C=NR); 2° amines have 1 N–H proton → neutral Enamine (C=C–NR₂). (Only an imine and enamine with the SAME formula interconvert as tautomers).

app.title: PLP Transamination Schiff Bases, Class I Aldolase & Strecker Amino Acid Synthesis

items.label: Pyridoxal Phosphate (Vitamin B6)
items.outcome: Lysine ε-NH₂ Forms Internal Schiff Base (Imine)
items.text: PLP uses its aldehyde to form an imine with amino acid substrates, acting as an electron sink to stabilize carbanion intermediates.

items.label: Wolff-Kishner Deoxygenation
items.outcome: C=O + H₂NNH₂ → Hydrazone + KOH/Δ → CH₂ + N₂↑
items.text: Converts an aldehyde or ketone into an alkane (C=O → CH₂) under basic conditions via a hydrazone intermediate.

items.label: Cyanohydrin Defense & Synthesis
items.text: Acid hydrolysis of a cyanohydrin converts –CN into –COOH (e.g., ethanal → lactic acid).

cards.rule: Aldehydes can be oxidized to carboxylic acids; ordinary ketones resist analogous oxidation without C–C cleavage. NaBH4 and LiAlH4 reduce aldehydes to primary alcohols and ketones to secondary alcohols. Hydride adds first, then oxygen is protonated in workup or by the medium. Suitable aqueous KMnO4 or Cr(VI) reagents (CrO3/acid or dichromate/acid) oxidize aldehydes. Tollens reagent is ammoniacal Ag(I), which is reduced to silver while an aldehyde becomes carboxylate in the basic medium; acid workup gives the acid. H2O2 can oxidize aldehydes under suitable conditions. Anhydrous PCC is commonly chosen to make aldehydes from primary alcohols while limiting overoxidation; it is not the only selective reagent.
cards.trap: Do not predict an alkane from ordinary hydride reduction of C=O. The oxygen remains in the alcohol. A positive aldehyde oxidation test is contextual evidence, not a complete structural identification. Tollens reagent is not a general primary-alcohol oxidant. Water, pH, workup and other oxidizable groups affect selectivity.
cards.app: Biological NADH-dependent carbonyl reductions transfer a hydride equivalent; the enzyme can control stereochemistry.

steps.label: 1. Aldehyde substrate
steps.text: Ethanal has a hydrogen on its carbonyl carbon, allowing ordinary oxidation to a carboxylic acid.

steps.label: 2. Oxidized product
steps.text: Ethanoic acid retains the two-carbon skeleton and adds a carbon–oxygen bond overall.

steps.label: 3. Reduced product
steps.text: The reduction product ethanol retains the same oxygen but has a single C–O bond and more C–H bonding.

rule.title: Diagnostic Aldehyde Oxidation (Tollens/Benedict) & Hydride Reduction (NaBH₄ vs. LiAlH₄)

items.label: Aldehyde-Specific Oxidation (Tollens, Fehling, Benedict)
items.text: Aldehydes have a weak C–H bond on the carbonyl carbon and oxidize easily to carboxylates (Ag⁺ → Ag⁰ mirror; Cu²⁺ blue → Cu₂O brick-red precipitate); simple ketones do NOT react.

items.label: Chemoselective Hydride Reduction (NaBH₄ vs. LiAlH₄)
items.text: Al is less electronegative than B, making the Al–H bond far more polar and hydride-donating: LiAlH₄ reduces esters/acids/amides, while mild NaBH₄ reduces only aldehydes/ketones (and acid chlorides).

items.label: Stereochemistry of Achiral Ketone Reduction
items.text: Hydride attacks the planar sp² ketone equally from the top (Re) and bottom (Si) faces, yielding a 50:50 RACEMIC mixture if a new stereocenter forms.

comparison: Ketones give NEGATIVE test (unless α-hydroxy tautomerizes)
Leaves Esters, Carboxylic Acids & Amides UNTOUCHED
Reduces Ald, Ket, Esters, Acids & Amides
Violently reacts with water; requires 2nd step H₃O⁺ workup

figure.caption: Aldehyde reduction to primary alcohol with a suitable hydride reagent, then protonation; schematic, not balanced.

cue.title: Carbonyl Redox Reagent & Stereochemical Outcome Selector
cue.prompt: What transformation or diagnostic test is being performed?

items.label: Distinguish Aldehyde from Ketone in Lab
items.text: Aldehyde is oxidized to RCOO⁻ while Ag⁺ is reduced to metallic Ag(s). (Note: α-hydroxy ketones in sugars give a positive test via enediol tautomerization!).

items.label: Reduce Ketone to 2° ROH Without Touching an Ester
items.text: Mild NaBH₄ selectively reduces the ketone C=O while the ester –COOR remains intact.

items.label: Track Where H Comes From in LiAlD₄ then H₂O
items.outcome: Deuterium (D) Bonds to Carbon; H Bonds to Oxygen!
items.text: Hydride/deuteride (D:⁻) attacks the electrophilic carbonyl CARBON; the aqueous workup protonates the alkoxide OXYGEN.

trap.title: Mixing LiAlH₄ with Water/Alcohol in Step 1 or Putting Workup H⁺ on Carbon

items.label: Common Trap
items.text: Writing "LiAlH₄ in MeOH" in a single step, or putting the H from H₃O⁺ onto the carbonyl carbon.

items.label: Correct Reasoning
items.text: LiAlH₄ reacts explosively with protic solvents (H:⁻ + H₂O → H₂↑); always run Step 1 in anhydrous ether/THF and Step 2 H₃O⁺ workup (which protonates O⁻).

app.title: Benedict Reducing-Sugar Test & Stereospecific Enzyme Reduction (LDH)

items.label: Benedict Test for Reducing Sugars
items.text: Any sugar with a free hemiacetal (glucose, fructose via enediol, maltose, lactose) opens to an aldehyde and tests positive; sucrose tests negative!

items.label: Lactate Dehydrogenase (LDH)
items.text: Unlike achiral NaBH₄ (which gives racemic (±)-lactate), chiral NADH inside LDH delivers hydride exclusively to one face of pyruvate!

items.label: Isotope Labeling with NaBD₄
items.text: Proves the mechanism: nucleophilic deuteride attacks C=O carbon first, while solvent protonates oxygen second.

stages.prompt: Select the atom attacked by a carbon nucleophile.
stages.explanation: The nucleophile attacks the carbonyl carbon.
hints: Locate the positively polarized end of C=O.

stages.prompt: As the new sigma bond forms, the C=O pi pair moves to…
stages.explanation: Moving the pi pair to O prevents carbon from exceeding an octet.
hints: Count the carbon bonds during attack.
O can carry the resulting negative charge.

stages.prompt: The immediate former-carbonyl geometry becomes approximately…
stages.explanation: Addition replaces the pi bond and gives four sigma directions around carbon.
